summary.title: Environmentally friendly and roll-processed flexible organic solar cells based on PM6:Y6
summary.authors: Marcial Fernández Castro; Jean Truer; Espíndola Rodríguez; Jens Wenzel
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the 'lab-to-fab gap' in Organic Solar Cells (OSCs) by demonstrating the fabrication of high-efficiency flexible devices using environmentally friendly, scalable slot-die coating. The authors utilized the high-performance PM6:Y6 non-fullerene acceptor system on flexible substrates, employing o-xylene as a green solvent without additives. A critical challenge identified was the temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA) of the PM6 donor, which necessitated a 'hot slot-die' process where the substrate, syringe, and coating head were heated to maintain ink fluidity. Through systematic optimization of coating temperature and active layer thickness, the team achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 6.3% for binary devices and 7.2% for ternary devices incorporating PCBM. The study highlights that coating at 100°C optimizes performance by balancing drying kinetics and molecular packing, avoiding the inhomogeneities caused by faster drying at higher temperatures. Furthermore, the introduction of PCBM enhanced charge dissociation and collection probabilities. The fabricated devices exhibited exceptional stability, retaining over 99% of their initial efficiency after more than 1000 hours of dark storage, validating the robustness of the open-air, roll-processed manufacturing approach for commercial scalability.

Executive Summary
This study addresses the 'lab-to-fab gap' in Organic Solar Cells (OSCs) by demonstrating the fabrication of high-efficiency flexible devices using environmentally friendly, scalable slot-die coating. The authors utilized the high-performance PM6:Y6 non-fullerene acceptor system on flexible substrates, employing o-xylene as a green solvent without additives. A critical challenge identified was the temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA) of the PM6 donor, which necessitated a 'hot slot-die' process where the substrate, syringe, and coating head were heated to maintain ink fluidity. Through systematic optimization of coating temperature and active layer thickness, the team achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 6.3% for binary devices and 7.2% for ternary devices incorporating PCBM. The study highlights that coating at 100°C optimizes performance by balancing drying kinetics and molecular packing, avoiding the inhomogeneities caused by faster drying at higher temperatures. Furthermore, the introduction of PCBM enhanced charge dissociation and collection probabilities. The fabricated devices exhibited exceptional stability, retaining over 99% of their initial efficiency after more than 1000 hours of dark storage, validating the robustness of the open-air, roll-processed manufacturing approach for commercial scalability.

Research Context
OSCs face a large efficiency gap between lab and industry processes. Spin-coating is inefficient for upscaling due to material waste. Slot-die coating is preferred for roll-to-roll manufacturing. PM6:Y6 systems show high efficiency but require specific processing. PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation requiring heat.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can PM6:Y6 OSCs be fabricated efficiently via slot-die coating? Does a green solvent system enable high performance? What coating temperature optimizes the TDA behavior of PM6? Does adding PCBM improve charge transport in ternary blends? Can open-air processed flexible devices maintain long-term stability?

Methodological Details
Active layer materials were purchased without purification. The flexible substrate is ITO-coated polyethylene terephthalate. A homemade roll-coater was used for layer deposition. The device geometry is inverted: ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. The ZnO ETL was coated at 75 °C with 0.06 mL/min flow. The AL was coated at varying temperatures from 60 to 120 °C. The drum speed was maintained at 1.5 m/min for AL coating. The solution flow rate for AL was 0.12 mL/min. MoO3 and Ag electrodes were thermally evaporated under vacuum. Devices had an approximate active area of 0.8 cm 2. Activation involved a reverse bias current of -5 V. Encapsulation used epoxy-based glue cured under UV light. J-V curves were measured with a Keithley 2400 source meter. A shadow mask defined an aperture area of 0.3996 cm 2. Statistics were based on averages of eight devices.

Procedures And Architectures
The ink remained hot via a heated tube to the slot-die head. The head, syringe, drum, and tube were kept at the same temperature. Annealing was performed at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The AL ratio was fixed at 1:1 for binary blends. Ternary blends used PCBM as a complementary acceptor. Ratios tested included [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1]. Absorbance was measured from 300 to 1100 nm. Thickness was measured using a DS95-50 AFM instrument. Light intensity was varied from 62.14 to 147.33 mW/cm 2. Deposition rate was monitored with an INFICON XTM/2 system.

Key Results
Optimal coating temperature was determined to be 100 °C. Coating at 120 °C resulted in the lowest average FF of 42.2%. The PCE saturated around 100 °C and did not improve further. The highest champion PCE for binary devices was 6.3%. The average PCE for binary devices at 217 nm thickness was 5.8%. The maximum short-circuit current density reached 17.3 mA/cm 2. The champion PCE for ternary devices was 7.2%. The average PCE for ternary devices was 6.7%. Ternary devices showed a 12% higher JSC than binary devices. The dissociation probability for binary devices was 93.7%. The collection probability for ternary devices reached 77.7%. Devices retained 99.4% of initial PCE after 1050 hours. Binary devices retained over 97% after 1500 hours.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Higher coating temperatures improved carrier collection efficiency. Temperatures above 100 °C caused material aggregation at edges. Reduced bimolecular recombination at 100 °C boosted performance. Thicker layers increased absorption but FF plateaued at 116 nm. PCBM addition created an energy cascade effect. Ternary blends enhanced exciton dissociation probability. Open-air processing led to high trap-assisted recombination. The results validate slot-die coating for industrial upscaling.

Contradictions And Limitations
No clear tendency was observed in S values for recombination. Devices were not prepared in a cleanroom or glovebox. High trap-assisted recombination was attributed to open-air processing.

Claims
Slot-die coating with hot slot-die parameters maximizes PM6:Y6 efficiency. Robustness And Ablation Notes
Annealing improved JSC for devices coated at 60 °C and 80 °C. Devices coated at 100 °C and 120 °C did not improve after annealing. The optimal thickness was found to be around 200 nm.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the chemical structures of PM6 and Y6. Figure 2 shows J-V curves and EQEs at different temperatures. Figure 3 shows box plots of PCE and FF evolution. Table 1 lists PV parameters extracted from J-V curves. Figure 7 compares photovoltaic parameters of binary and ternary devices.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration of high-efficiency flexible OSCs via slot-die coating. 2. The strongest evidence is the 99.4% efficiency retention after 1050 hours. 3. The future path involves transferring this technology to full roll-to-roll platforms.
